▸ Fix “Cannot use import statement outside a module” in JavaScript

💡 Fix the "Cannot use import statement outside a module" error by configuring ES module support in Node.js, TypeScript, and testing tools.

The "Cannot use import statement outside a module" error occurs when executing ES module (ESM) syntax within classic script or CommonJS contexts, requiring explicit runtime configuration such as adding `type="module"` to browser `<script>` tags or Node.js `package.json` files. Transitioning to native ESM removes traditional CommonJS globals like `__dirname` (replacing them with `import.meta.dirname`), mandates explicit file extensions on relative imports, and requires import attributes for non-JavaScript files like JSON. For TypeScript projects, execution issues can be resolved by using `tsx` instead of `ts-node` or configuring `tsconfig.json` with `"module": "NodeNext"`. Finally, testing environments impacted by this error can be fixed by adjusting Jest's Babel transforms and `transformIgnorePatterns`, or by migrating to Vitest for out-of-the-box ESM support.

📝 关键要点 (6 sections)
  • Understanding the Error: The error occurs when JavaScript runs as a classic browser script or CommonJS file, neither of which supports native import statements. Resolving it requires explicitly instructing the runtime environment to parse the file as an ES module.
  • Fixing Browser Scripts: Add type="module" to script tags to enable ES module syntax in the browser. Be aware that browser modules defer automatically, block file:// protocol access due to CORS, and require explicit file extensions.
  • Node.js Configuration Options: Enable ES modules in Node.js by adding "type": "module" to package.json or renaming files to the .mjs extension. Alternatively, stay in CommonJS by using require() or dynamic import() functions.
  • ES Module Quirks: Switching to ES modules removes CommonJS globals like require and __dirname, requiring modern replacements like import.meta.dirname. Relative imports also require explicit file extensions, and JSON imports require import attributes.
  • TypeScript Module Setup: Use tsx instead of ts-node to execute TypeScript files directly without module configuration issues. When building with tsc, set module to NodeNext in tsconfig.json to match package.json settings.
  • Jest and Vitest Solutions: Fix Jest CommonJS defaults by transforming code with Babel or adjusting transformIgnorePatterns for ESM node_modules. Switch to Vitest for out-of-the-box ES module support with minimal configuration.

▸ CSS calc(): How to Do Math in CSS (With Examples)

💡 CSS `calc()` enables dynamic arithmetic across mixed units to streamline responsive layouts and enhance custom property logic.

The CSS `calc()` function enables dynamic, runtime arithmetic within stylesheets, primary serving to evaluate expressions containing incompatible units like percentages, pixels, and viewport lengths. Using `calc()` requires strict adherence to parsing rules, including mandatory whitespace around addition and subtraction operators and the use of unitless scalar values for multiplication and division. Architecturally, it excels at solving complex layout offsets and combining with CSS custom properties to create derived design tokens or type unitless variables passed from JavaScript. While standard parentheses handle nested operational logic, modern CSS comparison functions (`min()`, `max()`, `clamp()`) extend this mathematical paradigm by supporting implicit arithmetic without requiring explicit `calc()` wrappers.

📝 关键要点 (6 sections)
  • Dynamic Layout Math: The CSS `calc()` function performs runtime arithmetic within stylesheets to create dynamic layouts. Its core strength lies in combining incompatible unit types, such as subtracting fixed pixel values from percentage or viewport lengths.
  • Syntax and Operator Rules: Addition and subtraction operators require surrounding whitespace to prevent browser parsing errors. Multiplication and division mandate plain numbers as scalar operands, and dividing by zero invalidates the CSS declaration.
  • Practical Layout Patterns: `calc()` solves complex layout scenarios like dynamically subtracting header heights using viewport units, distributing flexbox column gaps, and creating scroll offsets for sticky headers.
  • Integration with CSS Variables: Pairing `calc()` with custom properties allows developers to build derived spacing scales from a single source variable. This approach also allows unitless numbers set by JavaScript to be easily converted into typed CSS measurements.
  • Nesting Math Expressions: Standard parentheses can group complex operations inside a `calc()` block without writing explicit nested function calls. Browsers automatically resolve nested `calc()` functions introduced via CSS custom properties.
  • Comparison with Clamp Functions: While `calc()` computes specific values, functions like `min()`, `max()`, and `clamp()` establish dynamic value boundaries. These newer comparison functions support math directly without requiring an embedded `calc()` function.

▸ Why don’t more developers “use the platform”? | Read the Tea Leaves

💡 Developers often build redundant JavaScript abstractions, making refactoring back to native browser APIs vital for reducing codebase complexity.

Modern web developers frequently bypass native browser APIs due to historical habits formed during early browser fragmentation, combined with the superior developer ergonomics and documentation of framework ecosystems like React and npm. Additionally, engineers are often driven to re-implement platform capabilities in JavaScript by the psychological satisfaction of code ownership, career-advancing learning opportunities, and a reliance on imperative logic over declarative CSS. While building custom abstractions fosters individual technical growth, it often results in bloated, overly complex codebases that ignore built-in platform capabilities. Consequently, experienced software engineers deliver significant architectural value by identifying these unnecessary abstractions and refactoring redundant custom logic back to native platform features.

📝 关键要点 (7 sections)
  • The Platform Debate: While web advocates implore developers to use native browser APIs, many developers remain skeptical. Understanding why developers choose custom code over built-in platform features is key to bridging this gap.
  • Historical Browser Gaps: Historically, developers had to create custom solutions because browsers lacked standard features and evolved at different speeds. Libraries like jQuery were necessary to ensure consistency across fragmented browser environments.
  • Ecosystem and Documentation: Framework-centric ecosystems like React and npm encourage developers to reach for familiar components rather than raw platform APIs. Superior documentation and developer ergonomics on npm further incentivize using third-party libraries.
  • The Joy of Building: Building components from scratch offers developers a rewarding learning experience and a sense of ownership, known as the IKEA effect. Reinventing existing browser features like modal dialogs can feel more engaging than simply using built-in HTML tags.
  • Growth Through Customization: Creating custom libraries and polyfills often serves as a primary pathway for developers to gain deep technical expertise. Filling platform gaps can motivate developers to eventually contribute directly to official browser standards.
  • CSS Ignorance and Workarounds: Developers often re-implement native layout and styling features in JavaScript due to a lack of deep CSS knowledge or past browser limitations. Imperative JavaScript logic is frequently favored over learning complex or historical CSS paradigms.
  • Universal Platform Skepticism: Avoiding native platform capabilities is common across software engineering and often results in overly complex code. Experienced engineers frequently add value by replacing custom logic with out-of-the-box platform features.
